blocks.text: Drawing on this, then, they have the chariot of Ceres drawn by winged dragons. Orpheus in the Hymn to Ceres:
Ἅρμα δρακοντείοισιν ὑποζεύξασα χαλινοῖς, [Harma drakonteioisin hypozeuxasa chalinois,]
Yoking the reins of (winged) dragons to the chariot. Ovid, Metamorphoses book 5, Fable 11:
— — The fertile goddess set twin snakes to her chariot, curbed their mouths with reins, and was borne through the air between heaven and earth.
And in book 4 of the Fasti:
— — she yoked bridled snakes to her chariot, and dry-shod wanders over the waters of the sea.
And below, [III, 230] — — — and she passes over to the dragons, and Ceres is raised aloft on the winged axle.
Claudian, book 1 On the Rape of Proserpina:
— — — guiding the sinuous limbs of dragons, which mark the clouds, passable to them, with their winged course [col. 434] and moisten the reins with gentle poison.
Borne in this very chariot into Scythia, Triptolemus said to Lyncus, king of Scythia, in Ovid at the place cited above:
— — — I came neither by ship over the waves, nor on foot over the lands: the open air lay passable before me.
That is, of Ceres
Δίφρον ἐχιδνήεντα δι᾽ ἠέρος ἡνιοχεύων, Στικτὰ φερεσταχύων ἐπεμάστιε νῶτα δρακόντων, [Diphron echidnēenta di᾽ ēeros hēniocheuōn, Stikta pherestachyōn epemastie nōta drakontōn,]

Driving the chariot through the air, he lashed the spotted backs of the ear-bearing dragons. So Nonnus, book 13 of the Dionysiaca. For Ceres sent him, borne by winged dragons, through the whole world to show men the use of grain. So teach Hyginus, Fable 147, and book 2 of the Astronomica, on Ophiuchus; Servius on book 1 of the Georgics; Phornutus in the book On the Nature of the Gods, chapter On Ceres; and not a few others. To say nothing of Medea, whom they feign to have received such a chariot from her father, the Sun. The Scholiast on Euripides in the Argument of the Medea: Μήδεια δὲ, τοὺς ἑαυτῆς παῖδας ἀποκτείνασα, ἐφ᾽ ἅρματος δρακόντων πτερωτῶν ἔποχος γενομένη, ἀποδιδράσκει εἰς Ἀθήνας [Mēdeia de, tous heautēs paidas apokteinasa, eph᾽ harmatos drakontōn pterōtōn epochos genomenē, apodidraskei eis Athēnas]. This is taken from Apollodorus at the end of book 1 of the Bibliotheca. Hence of the same woman Ovid, Metamorphoses book 7, Fable 2:

Not in vain: a chariot drawn by the necks of winged dragons is there; the chariot had come down from the sky. As soon as she mounted it and stroked the bridled necks of the dragons, and shook the light reins with her hands, she is swept on high. — — —
And Fable 5:
Had she not gone into the air on winged serpents, she would not have escaped punishment. — — —
And Fable 20:
At last on viperine wings she reached Ephyraean Pirene. — — — [III, 231] And Fable 21:
Carried off from here by Titanian dragons, she enters the Palladian citadel. — — —

Nor is it surprising that Circe is sometimes borne in this same chariot, since she too was a daughter of the Sun and the sister of Medea. Accordingly in Apollonius (Argonautica book 3, line 308) Circe is brought to Hesperia, that is Italy,
— — πατρὸς ἐν ἅρμασιν Ἡελίοιο, [patros en harmasin Ēelioio,]
in the chariot of her father, the Sun. The excellent Scholiast reports that he has this from Hesiod. And Valerius Flaccus, book 7:
— — as the winged dragons carried off Circe.
And below in the same place:
— — — was Circe at last scarcely restored, harsh to your people, whom flight drove hence with a pair of serpents? — — —

But that ships are signified by the name of dragons is taught by those very ancients: as in Eusebius' Chronicle the most celebrated writer Philochorus, when he reports that under Celeus, king of Eleusis, Triptolemus μακρῷ πλοίῳ προβαλόντα ταῖς πόλεσι τὸν σῖτον διαδοῦναι· ὑπονοεῖσθαι δὲ πτερωτὸν ὄφιν εἶναι τὴν ναῦν, ἔχειν δέ τι καὶ τοῦ σχήματος [makrō ploiō probalonta tais polesi ton siton diadounai; hyponoeisthai de pterōton ophin einai tēn naun, echein de ti kai tou schēmatos], having been carried in a long ship, distributed grain to the cities; and that the ship is signified by the winged serpent, since its shape is in some respect similar. Add, if you like, that a ship could be marked with the name Dragon which had a dragon as its ensign: as in Plutarch, in the book On the Virtues of Women, the pirate Chimarrus, slain by Bellerophon, ἔπλει πλοίῳ λέοντα μὲν ἔχοντι πρώραθεν ἐπίσημον, ἐκ δὲ πρύμνης δράκοντα [eplei ploiō leonta men echonti prōrathen episēmon, ek de prymnēs drakonta], sailed in a ship that had a lion on the prow and a dragon on the stern as its ensign. And in Euripides, Iphigenia in Aulis, the Boeotian ships had as their sign Cadmus
Χρύσεον δράκοντ᾽ ἔχων Ἀμφὶ ναῶν κόρυμβα· [Chryseon drakont᾽ echōn Amphi naōn korymba;]

holding a golden dragon on the beaks of the ships. To the same point belongs the fact that in the Fables [col. 435] those who are borne by dragons set out only from coastal places and only to coastal places. Thus Ceres, seeking Proserpina, after she had travelled over all Sicily without dragons, at last came also to the shores of the island:
